Iran’s Victory Parade Has a Pension Problem

Iran may be winning the war’s political afterlife — which is not the same thing as winning the war.

The U.S.-Israeli campaign inflicted major damage on Iranian military, industrial and nuclear-related targets. 

But the Islamic Republic survived. Its governing structure held. Its missile capacity endured. 

And Tehran turned the Strait of Hormuz from a vulnerability into a bargaining chip aimed at the global economy. Regime change, widely understood as a key ambition behind the campaign, did not happen.

That survival is the regime’s victory narrative. America and Israel brought superior firepower; Iran emerged battered, more radicalized and still sitting at the entrance to the Gulf. 

Tehran can now negotiate shipping arrangements with Oman, demand terms from Washington and present persistence itself as strategic genius. Formal Iranian control over part of Hormuz would be a clear gain for Tehran and a serious loss for Washington.

The American side has a different problem. Washington wants an end to the war. Jerusalem fears that the price of ending it will be paid in Israeli security, in Lebanon, Syria and Gaza. 

The nuclear issue, once marketed as the central justification, has become one file among many in a larger attempt to escape an escalating conflict without calling it retreat.

Iranian state media, naturally, declares Trump defeated. The president says this is the best time for a deal because Tehran is seen as the winner. 

That is what governments say after absorbing blows they could not prevent: survival becomes victory; damaged infrastructure becomes proof of resistance; a closed waterway becomes sovereignty.

But even victorious states have citizens. In Iran, pensioners are still protesting. The regime has secured a stronger bargaining position abroad while failing, with remarkable consistency, to make life bearable at home.

The Islamic Republic may have survived the war. Its retirees are still waiting to survive the peace.

📣 Brazil stablecoins face IMF scrutiny as crypto flows outpace capital 

🌐 IMF has called for closer oversight of Brazil’s stablecoin market as cross-border crypto flows outpace traditional capital movements. The report says cross-border crypto transactions have increased faster than conventional capital flows and now require closer regulatory attention because of their growing links with the country’s financial system. The assessment says stablecoin purchases respond much more strongly to global financial shocks than traditional portfolio investment or foreign direct investment. 

🔔 Based on the IMF’s analysis, purchases of dollar-backed stablecoins are two to three times more sensitive to external market events, raising concerns over how quickly international volatility could spread through crypto markets. Brazil has emerged as one of the world’s more active crypto markets, with stablecoins accounting for a significant share of digital asset activity. The IMF said the country’s crypto ecosystem has become increasingly connected with the traditional financial sector, making regulatory oversight more important as adoption continues to rise.

⚠️ The report acknowledges that Banco Central do Brasil (BCB) has already introduced measures to regulate crypto asset service providers. Even so, the IMF said several areas still need stronger rules, including customer asset protection, stablecoin issuance requirements, and compliance with anti-money laundering (AML) and counter-terrorist financing (CFT) standards.
